name: Dashboarding Best Practices
description: This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building dashboarding — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary dashboarding tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.
content:
This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building dashboarding — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary dashboarding tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Keep dashboarding outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
2. Measure before optimizing any dashboarding bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
3. Validate dashboarding outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
4. When dashboarding decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
5. Document any non-obvious dashboarding decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
6. Re-check edge cases relevant to dashboarding (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
7. Prefer the simplest dashboarding approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
8. State assumptions about dashboarding explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of dashboarding correctness.
- Avoid introducing new dashboarding abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not skip documenting dashboarding assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not apply generic dashboarding advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not silently drop dashboarding edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for dashboarding, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
